faqs.question: Which song is actually played on Ganesh Chaturthi?
faqs.answer: One is fixed and the rest are chosen. The fixed one is the Marathi aarti Sukhkarta Dukhharta, attributed to Samarth Ramdas (1608–1682), sung at the opening of the puja and then twice a day for the length of the festival. Film songs, bhajans and dhol-tasha are all optional and belong to other moments.

faqs.question: Is there one song I really have to know before the festival?
faqs.answer: Yes — Sukhkarta Dukhharta. It is the only item a room will expect you to already know, and it is the one thing a playlist cannot cover for you, because it is sung live rather than played.

faqs.question: What's the difference between an aarti, a bhajan and a kirtan?
faqs.answer: An aarti is short, sung standing, and tied to the waving of the lamp at a fixed point in the puja. A bhajan is a devotional song with no fixed slot — sing one for forty minutes or skip it. A kirtan is a narrated performance in which a kirtankar tells a story across an evening and sings within it.

faqs.question: How many times a day is the Ganpati aarti sung?
faqs.answer: Twice — morning and evening — for the whole festival. The repetition is the mechanism: by around the third day everyone in the house knows the words without having read them off anything.

faqs.question: Can I play Bollywood songs in front of the Ganpati idol?
faqs.answer: Play them, but not in the aarti slot. "Deva Shree Ganesha" from Agneepath (2012) is a good festival song and it belongs on the pandal system or in the car on the way to a visarjan — not in the ninety seconds when the lamp is going round.

faqs.question: What music is played during the visarjan procession?
faqs.answer: Traditionally dhol-tasha rather than recorded music. Since the 2016 Bombay High Court orders on the noise rules, DJs with loudspeakers and generators mounted on trucks have been banned from processions in Mumbai, though the ban is not always observed.

faqs.question: How loud can a Ganesh pandal legally play music in Maharashtra?
faqs.answer: The permitted limit in a residential area is 55 decibels. Awaaz Foundation's measurements during Mumbai's 2022 processions found that limit violated across the city, including 115 dB at Babulnath and a 120.2 dB peak at Opera House past midnight.

faqs.question: Do the songs have to be in Marathi, or is Hindi fine?
faqs.answer: The fixed aarti is Marathi, and that one is sung as it is. The evening bhajan and kirtan slot is where language varies legitimately — Hindi, Telugu and Kannada singing are all ordinary practice depending on the household, and nobody's version is wrong there.

faqs.question: When is Ganesh Chaturthi in 2026, and when is the visarjan?
faqs.answer: Ganesh Chaturthi is Monday 14 September 2026 and the Anant Chaturdashi visarjan is Friday 25 September 2026. The conventional "ten days" spans eleven or twelve calendar days in most years, because the count follows the tithi rather than the date.

faqs.question: What do I do if nobody in the room knows the words?
faqs.answer: Get the words in front of them on a phone, not on a printed sheet — 49.6% of SubhSandesh's shared-page views are phone opens and 49.8% are on a touch device. But keep one voice leading; twenty people each reading their own screen fragments the singing.

faqs.question: Is dhol-tasha safe for the people playing it?
faqs.answer: Less than most players assume. A study of 50 dhol-tasha players aged 18 to 35 in Pune district notes that these musicians are routinely exposed to levels above 85 dB during Ganesh Chaturthi processions, and that awareness of hearing loss among them is under-researched.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganesh Chaturthi Songs: What to Play on Each of the Ten Days

Ganesh Chaturthi songs fall into two categories that every playlist article merges, and separating them is the whole job. Exactly one item is fixed liturgy: **सुखकर्ता दुःखहर्ता**, *Sukhkarta Dukhharta*, the Marathi aarti attributed to Samarth Ramdas (1608–1682), sung at the start of Ganesha puja across Maharashtra and repeated twice a day for the length of the festival.

Everything else — bhajans, kirtan, film songs, the dhol-tasha at the visarjan — is optional, regional and generational. In 2026 the festival opens on **Monday 14 September** and the Anant Chaturdashi visarjan is **Friday 25 September**.

SubhSandesh has measured **3,894 personalised pages** built since 12 March 2026 across 15 page types, of which **96.0% (3,737)** are published and shared, and **49.6% of the 46,005 recorded views** arrive on a phone — the constraint that decides how twenty people read the same words at once. Below, each song sits at the moment it belongs to.

## The one fixed point: an aarti composed before 1682

Sukhkarta Dukhharta is not one option among ten. It belongs to the "most standard and almost universal" set of aarti songs sung at the opening of Ganesha worship in Maharashtra, [attributed to the seventeenth-century saint Samarth Ramdas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhakarta_Dukhaharta) — a text roughly 350 years old, with no author's discretion left in it.

That matters practically. A liturgical item is performed at a fixed point, in a fixed form, whether or not anyone likes it that day; a repertoire item is chosen.

Listicles that rank the aarti at number four between two film songs have quietly recategorised it as a choice. If you learn one thing before 14 September, learn this aarti — it is the only item here a room will expect you to already know.

## Bhajan, aarti and kirtan are three different forms, and only one is timed

An **aarti** accompanies the waving of the lamp: short, sung standing, tied to a specific moment in the puja. A **bhajan** is a devotional song with no fixed slot — sing one for forty minutes or not at all. A **kirtan** is a narrated performance rather than a song, in which a *kirtankar* tells a story across an evening, singing within it.

Anna Christine Schultz's open-access study of Marathi *naradiya* kirtan, [published in Open Access Musicology Volume 3 in 2025](https://www.openaccessmusicology.com/essays/marathi-kirtan-before-and-after-the-classical), reads the 1925 Marathi biography of the nineteenth-century kirtankar Govindbuva Hoshing and shows how Brahmin performers selectively absorbed Hindustani raga, tala and improvisation while rejecting that music's secular performance contexts. Her argument is that the devotional and the classical were separated by a boundary people drew, not by sound.

Ganeshotsav's music has always been sorted, not shuffled — the same instinct that keeps a film song out of the aarti.

## Song mapped to moment, 14 to 25 September 2026

The conventional "ten days" spans eleven or twelve calendar days in most years, because the count follows the tithi and not the date — 2026 runs Monday 14 September to Friday 25 September. Household immersions on the day-and-a-half, fifth or seventh day are ordinary regional practice, so not every mandap uses all five slots below.

### 1. Sthapana, Monday 14 September — the aarti, and nothing before it

The idol is installed and the first aarti is sung. Nothing else plays until the aarti has been sung once. If a speaker is on when the idol arrives, turn it off — the single most common mistake at a first-year household mandap.

### 2. Every morning and every evening — the same aarti, twice a day

Two aartis a day for the whole festival. The repetition is the point: by the third day everyone in the house knows the words, which is exactly what an unfamiliar text needs. Nothing on a playlist substitutes for this slot.

### 3. Evenings, days two to nine — bhajan and kirtan, where the region shows

The movable half of the festival, and the only slot with real local character. A Konkan household runs abhangs; a Pune building's mandal may book a kirtankar for one evening; a Hyderabad or Bengaluru flat will often sing in Telugu or Kannada. Nobody's version is wrong here.

### 4. Daytime, public pandals — film songs and the 55 dB residential ceiling

The pandal loudspeaker is a different venue with different rules. Sumaira Abdulali, reporting Awaaz Foundation's own measurements, found Mumbai's residential permitted limit of **55 decibels** [violated across the city during the 2022 Ganesh processions](https://citizenmatters.in/rising-noise-levels-ganesh-visarjan-mumbai/), with **115 dB at Babulnath** on the fifth day of visarjan and **112 dB in Bandra**. Film songs live here, not at the aarti.

### 5. Anant Chaturdashi, Friday 25 September — the procession

Dhol-tasha, not recorded music, is the traditional procession sound. Abdulali logged a peak of **120.2 dB at Opera House** past midnight on the final visarjan day of 2022, against **93.1 dB** on the tenth visarjan day of 2021 and **121.3 dB in 2019** — same route, wildly different years.

## What belongs where: four settings against a 55 dB residential limit

| Setting | What to play | Fixed or chosen | Measured sound reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Household mandap, aarti slot | Sukhkarta Dukhharta, sung live | Fixed liturgy | Unamplified; well under the 55 dB residential limit |
| Household mandap, evening | Bhajans, abhangs, one kirtan | Chosen, regional | Unamplified; no legal exposure |
| Public pandal, daytime | Film and devotional recordings | Chosen, generational | 55 dB limit; 115 dB recorded at Babulnath, 2022 |
| Visarjan procession | Dhol-tasha pathak | Chosen, traditional | 120.2 dB peak at Opera House, 2022; 93.1 dB in 2021 |

The fourth column is the one no playlist article carries, and it is why the first two rows are not interchangeable with the last two. A study of young dhol-tasha players in Pune district — 50 participants aged 18 to 35, each with five or more years' playing experience — notes routine exposure [above 85 dB during Ganesh Chaturthi processions](https://www.ijaresm.com/awareness-of-noise-induced-hearing-loss-among-young-dhol-tasha-players-in-maharashtra) and that hearing-loss awareness among them is under-researched. Only the abstract was readable, so its awareness figures are not quoted here.

## Film songs from 2012 onward: correct in the pandal, wrong at the aarti

The track every listicle opens with is "Deva Shree Ganesha" from *Agneepath* (2012), composed by Ajay–Atul. It is a genuinely good festival song and it is fourteen years old, which makes it a *generational* marker: it is what someone who was a teenager in 2012 hears as Ganpati music, and not what a grandparent hears.

That is not a reason to skip it, only a reason to know its slot. Play it on the pandal system, or in the car on the way to a visarjan — not in the ninety seconds when the lamp is going round.

## Getting twenty people onto the same words: 49.6% of them arrive on a phone

The practical failure is never repertoire. It is that six people know the aarti's second verse and fourteen are humming.

SubhSandesh's numbers say the fix has to be phone-shaped: **49.6% of shared pages are opened on a phone (22,817 of 46,005 views)** and **49.8% of all views are on a touch device**, both measured 9 September 2026. A printed sheet does not survive twenty pairs of hands; a link does.

There is a timing fact worth naming, with its limits stated plainly. Across both rakhi collections SubhSandesh measured **n = 89** pages against the festival date in IST calendar days: **49.4% (44 of 89)** were built on the day itself, **27.0%** the day before, and **not one of the 89** more than seven days ahead — median lead time **0 days**.

Two caveats. That measurement is **Raksha Bandhan, which fell on 28 August 2026 — a different festival, and a one-day one**; Ganesh Chaturthi runs ten days to Anant Chaturdashi, so the same shape is *suggestive*, not measured for this festival. And **n = 89 is small**: no per-template or per-region rate can be derived from it, and no count of Ganesh pages projected from it.

Read against that, the instruction is unglamorous: settle the aarti and two or three bhajans now, and expect the sharing to happen on the morning of the 14th. If you want a page carrying the words, [browse the SubhSandesh templates](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

For the film-song half of the festival there is a closer fit — [the Dedication radio-show page](https://subhsandesh.in/dedication) lets you introduce a track in your own recorded voice, which a shared playlist link never does. To see how a festival greeting page behaves, [the Holi greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/holi) is the closest live example.

## Where a shareable page is the wrong choice: 144 of 3,894 pages, 3.7%

Be clear about what this platform is. Occasion-dated pages — every festival plus every wedding type — are **144 of 3,894 pages, just 3.7%**; the other 96.3% are romantic pages between two people.

SubhSandesh has **no Ganesh page-creation data at all**, because that template is not live at the time of writing. Anyone calling Ganesh page-building a mass behaviour here is reading a number that does not exist.

A link is also the wrong tool for the aarti itself. Twenty people singing together need one voice leading and the rest following; a screen each fragments that. Use a page for the invitation, the *darshan* timings and the words for people who do not know them — then put the phones down when the lamp is lit.

Ganeshotsav is official state business now, too: Maharashtra's Cultural Affairs Minister Ashish Shelar [announced in the Legislative Assembly in July 2025 that Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav is a state festival](https://www.newsonair.gov.in/maharashtra-declares-sarvajanik-ganeshotsav-as-state-festival), with the state bearing organising costs. Public music here is regulated, funded and measured.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Anna Christine Schultz, "Marathi Kirtan Before and After 'The Classical'", *Open Access Musicology* Volume 3, 2025 — open-access scholarly essay on Marathi naradiya kirtan.
- Sumaira Abdulali, "Soaring noise levels during Ganesh festival underlines the need for citizen action", *Citizen Matters*, 20 September 2022 — Awaaz Foundation's measured decibel readings at Mumbai's Ganesh visarjan.
- Sharanya Jothiprakash Shetty and Vini Abhijith Gupta, "Awareness of Noise-Induced Hearing loss among Young Dhol Tasha Players in Maharashtra", *IJARESM* 13(1), January 2025 — abstract only was readable.
- "Maharashtra declares Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav as state festival", *Akashvani News*, 11 July 2025.
- "Sukhakarta Dukhaharta", English Wikipedia — used only to verify the Devanagari spelling and the attribution to Samarth Ramdas.

failed.item: At least one table column uses first-party data
failed.why: STRUCTURAL. The comparison table's four columns are setting, repertoire, fixed-vs-chosen and a measured sound reference; all the numbers in it are third-party (Awaaz Foundation via Citizen Matters). SubhSandesh has no per-setting, per-venue or per-festival measurement that could fill a column here — and specifically no Ganesh page-creation data at all, because the /happy-ganesh-chaturthi template is not live. Adding a first-party column would mean inventing a dimension the data does not have. Closes only when the Ganesh template ships and enough pages exist to segment by anything.

failed.item: Slug short, hyphenated, lowercase, no stop words
failed.why: The assigned slug `ganesh-chaturthi-songs-and-bhajans` carries the stop word 'and'. Fixed by ASSIGNMENTS.json (assignments[2]) and already verified free on Strapi today; changing it would break the assignment contract and void the availability check, so it is left as assigned rather than silently altered.

failed.item: No source passes the **swap test** — none could sit unchanged in a different keyword's post in this batch
failed.why: Four of the five sources are lane-specific and would not transplant. The exception is the newsonair.gov.in state-festival announcement, which is general Ganeshotsav news and could sit unchanged in another Ganesh post in this wave. It is kept because it is the only verified support for the claim that public Ganeshotsav music is now state-funded and regulated, but the item is failed rather than claimed. It is also this post's single generic government statistic, so the two constraints trade against each other. Closes if a music-specific government source is found — the reported 'Bhajani Mandals eligible for a grant of up to Rs 5 crore' detail would qualify, but it was not verifiable on the newsonair page itself.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this over the two ranked listicles for one reason: it is the only page that treats the aarti as a different category of object from a film song, and then answers "what do I play, and when" against the sthapana / twice-daily aarti / visarjan clock with dated third-party decibel figures per venue. The listicles are unsourced countdowns with no ritual sequencing and no numbers to supersede, so the fact density is genuinely one-sided. What it cannot overcome: the SERP is dominated by streaming catalogues (Saregama, Spotify, JioSaavn) whose intent is a play queue, not prose, and SubhSandesh's domain authority sits far below those platforms — a text page can only win the narrower "what belongs where" question, not the head query. Three audit items are failed rather than papered over: the comparison table carries no first-party column because no such measurement exists (there is no Ganesh page data at all, the template is not live), the assigned slug carries a stop word, and the newsonair state-festival source would transplant to another Ganesh post in this wave. The India-localised SERP could not be corroborated on a second engine today, though at 0 shared articles the gate was nowhere near its threshold. No claim is made about whether this will rank.
